children: JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab are blocking unauthorized artificial-intelligence agents from accessing customer accounts and money. The companies say their policies are intended to protect clients.

The moves, detailed in earnings calls this week, may also blunt concerns among investors that AI cash optimizing tools could threaten low-cost deposits that banks and brokerage firms rely on. The concern is that AI agents will automatically move cash from low-paying accounts to higher-paying alternatives elsewhere, sparking mass flows of cash and pressuring earnings.
But that scenario may not come to fruition if AI agents can't get past the gatekeepers.

On JPMorgan's Tuesday earnings call, an analyst asked management to address concerns that AI agents will take deposits out of JPMorgan. CFO Jeremy Barnum said the company was against allowing AI agents to gain access to money and move it in customers' bank accounts through credential sharing. "We have a long record of being against that way of doing things, screen scraping, et cetera," he said. "It's not secure."

Barnum said the company is blocking AI agents from doing that to protect customers and the bank. "It's important that customers understand that if they give up their credentials to the agent and the agent does something that they don't want, that's going to be on them," he said.

Such a situation would be far from ideal, he said. JPMorgan is trying to give customers AI tools in a safe manner. "In the big picture, trust is clearly an asset and we spent decades building it," he said. "And as I said previously, we like our hand in that respect."

A JPMorgan spokeswoman says customer protection is the bank's priority. "When we detect a third-party agent attempting to access accounts by obtaining customers' banking credentials we do not allow it."

With regard to Schwab, CEO Rick Wurster outlined what AI capabilities his company is providing customers on his company's Thursday morning earnings call. "First, we are blocking unauthorized agents who try to log in on behalf of clients. It is not a safe way for our clients to access Schwab, and we are blocking it to protect clients and our firm," he said.
Wurster added that Schwab hasn't had to block many AI bots because few clients have attempted to access their accounts that way.

The Westlake, Texas-based company recently launched Charley, an AI bot, to answer customer questions and take limited actions on their behalf, such as changing an address. Charley is powered by outside AI models and could evolve into a more powerful tool. "Over time, Charley will do a lot more, ultimately becoming an important front door to Schwab," Wurster said.

Schwab also recently joined with tech company Anthropic to offer independent financial advisors a suite of AI tools called Claude for Financial Advisors. In a pilot test, Schwab is allowing a small group of active traders to securely connect their AI model to a Schwab account to support their investment strategies.

Investors' AI worries have repeatedly weighed on bank and brokerage stocks over the past year, with concerns generally centered on AI posing a threat to companies' earnings. In September, investors dumped bank and brokerage stocks after Meta unveiled Muse, an AI assistant that can perform tasks on behalf of customers, such as shopping. Investors' anxieties center on whether Muse or something like it could help Americans optimize their cash holdings, automatically transferring idle dollars from low-paying bank accounts to higher-paying alternatives elsewhere. That would pressure net interest income, a key source of profits at financial institutions.
It's a potentially worrisome scenario for financial stocks, but one that has yet to materialize.

Earlier this week, Wells Fargo CEO Charles Scharf said that scenario of mass cash movement has become "completely overdone." Speaking on his company's earnings call, he questioned whether clients would really give AI agents free rein with their cash.

"The idea that consumers are going to give the power to an agent to act on their behalf unilaterally and move money around to institutions that they don't know, they don't understand, where they don't understand the terms of the accounts they're moving it to and all those types of things, I think it's a long ways away," Scharf said.
